lessons.title: Storage foundations: blocks, files, RAID and multipathing
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Block storage exposes addressable blocks to a host, which normally supplies its own filesystem or volume manager. File storage exposes a filesystem service such as NFS. A storage network's job is not merely to carry packets: the host must access the intended data with correct identity, ordering, durability and recovery behaviour. Latency distributions and queueing often matter more than peak bandwidth.

RAID addresses some device failures inside a storage system; multipathing addresses alternative host-to-storage paths; replication maintains another data copy under a defined consistency model; backup supports recovery from historical states. These controls are complementary. Mirroring can faithfully copy corrupted or malicious writes. Two paths through one switch do not provide switch independence. A snapshot may share the same physical and administrative failure domain as its source.

Evaluate workload IOPS, request size, read/write mix, queue depth, cache behaviour and sustained tail latency. A cache-assisted benchmark can exaggerate steady-state capability. For failover, inspect application I/O completion and data consistency in addition to path state. A surviving session that stalls longer than the application timeout is not successful continuity.

### Engineering decisions

**What is the nominal payload rate for the stated workload?** 390.625 MiB/s. 50000 times 8192 bytes divided by 1048576 gives 390.625 MiB/s.

**Why are the two paths not switch-independent?** Both traverse the same SAN switch. A single switch failure can remove both paths.

**Why did replication not protect the deleted data?** It copied the logical deletion. Replication preserves a defined current-state relationship, not necessarily history.

**What limits the short benchmark's conclusion?** Its data fits in cache and may not exercise steady-state storage. Sustained workload and working-set behaviour can differ.

**What does multipathing primarily provide?** Alternative host-to-storage path management. It does not by itself create historical backups.

**What distinguishes NFS from block access?** NFS exposes file-service operations. A block target exposes blocks for the host's storage stack.

**Why include application timeout in failover acceptance?** Path recovery slower than the timeout may still fail the service. Transport recovery must meet workload continuity requirements.

**Which protection is specifically aimed at a historical recovery point?** A retained and tested backup or suitable protected version history. Recovery from logical damage requires an earlier usable state.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Fibre Channel login, addressing and name services
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Fibre Channel has its own addressing and fabric services. A WWPN is a persistent port identity; an FCID is a fabric-assigned address used for forwarding. During fabric login, an N-port establishes its relationship with the fabric and obtains addressing appropriate to that fabric. The name server records reachable registered devices and attributes. Device-to-device login and upper-layer exchanges occur after the relevant fabric prerequisites.

A VSAN partitions logical fabrics on supported MDS infrastructure. Domain identifiers are part of FC addressing, so fabric merges need compatible domain assignments and policy. A physical ISL can be up while a particular VSAN is isolated or not carried. The fabric's principal-switch and domain assignment process is not equivalent to Ethernet spanning tree.

Trace a missing target from physical signal and port mode through VSAN membership, FLOGI, FCNS registration, zoning and storage authorization. An FCNS entry proves registration, not that the host has permission to every LUN. A WWPN seen in an old configuration can differ from the replacement adapter's current identity. Keep device aliases readable, but remember that the underlying identity and active policy govern forwarding.

### Engineering decisions

**What does the host's FLOGI establish?** It logged into VSAN 20 and obtained fabric addressing. It does not prove access to the target in VSAN 30.

**Why is the target absent from the host's normal fabric view?** The target is registered in a different VSAN. Logical fabric separation is an independent boundary.

**How does an FCID differ from a WWPN?** FCID is fabric-assigned forwarding address; WWPN is port identity. The distinction matters during moves and fabric changes.

**What does FCNS registration prove?** The device has registered in that fabric's name service. It does not establish array LUN masking or application I/O.

**Why inspect VSAN carriage on an ISL?** A physical link may not carry the required logical fabric. Link-up alone does not establish per-VSAN connectivity.

**What issue can a fabric-domain conflict cause?** A problematic merge or isolated fabric relationship. Domain identity must be consistent with fabric rules.

**Why verify a replacement HBA's actual WWPN?** Authorization may still reference the old port identity. Inventory assumptions can differ from the effective initiator.

**What is the last meaningful acceptance stage?** Correct application I/O to the intended authorized volume. Earlier fabric success does not establish service correctness.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Use a supported MDS lab with an initiator and disposable target volume, or an authorized provider lab. This workbook's WWPNs and outputs are synthetic and its commands were not executed on equipment here. Pin NX-OS, switch model, optic and array/HBA compatibility. Keep A/B fabrics independent unless a separately approved design requires otherwise.

**Requirement.** Initiator LAB-HOST may access only LAB-TARGET in VSAN20 and only the intended disposable LUN through array masking. A second unrelated initiator must remain denied. A single-fabric outage must preserve required application I/O through the separately commissioned other fabric.

Illustrative logical construction:

```text
vsan database
  vsan 20 name LAB_A
  vsan 20 interface fc1/1
  vsan 20 interface fc1/2
interface fc1/1
  switchport mode F
  no shutdown
interface fc1/2
  switchport mode F
  no shutdown
device-alias database
  device-alias name LAB-HOST pwwn 20:00:00:25:b5:00:00:11
  device-alias name LAB-TARGET pwwn 50:00:00:25:b5:00:00:21
  exit
device-alias commit
zone name LAB-HOST-TO-TARGET vsan 20
  member pwwn 20:00:00:25:b5:00:00:11
  member pwwn 50:00:00:25:b5:00:00:21
zoneset name LAB-ACTIVE vsan 20
  member LAB-HOST-TO-TARGET
```

Before activation, compare the proposed full database with the actual active zoneset. The example intentionally uses explicit WWPN members while creating aliases for readable identity records, avoiding an assumption about device-alias mode. In a real existing fabric, do not activate a tiny lab zoneset that omits production zones. Use the selected release's supported transaction and CFS procedure, coordinate existing session ownership and activate only the reviewed complete intended policy for the isolated VSAN.

Illustrative activation command for this isolated lab is `zoneset activate name LAB-ACTIVE vsan 20`. Confirm the exact syntax and mode for the selected platform. Record the active policy before and after. Read the supported forms of `show flogi database`, `show fcns database`, `show zoneset active vsan 20`, `show device-alias database`, VSAN/port state and interface error/credit counters.

**Interpretation ladder.** FLOGI shows initiator attachment and FCID assignment. FCNS shows registered fabric identity. Active zoning permits the communication pair. Array masking exposes a volume. Host discovery/multipathing presents the intended device. Only an application read/write with integrity checks demonstrates useful storage service. A management ping to the array is not a substitute for this chain.

**Faults.** Replace the initiator WWPN in a proposed zone with a retired identity; leave a correct zone unactivated; remove the required VSAN from an ISL; disable or constrain required upstream NPIV in a supported NPV exercise; and analyze supplied credit/CRC time series. Introduce one fault at a time. Do not intentionally corrupt valuable data; use disposable volumes and known test patterns.

For credit diagnosis, compare deltas over the incident interval. Persistent transmit-credit-zero time with clean CRC and a slow receiver suggests a different mechanism from rising CRC/link resets. For distance, estimate the in-flight byte budget and check supported credit allocation. A simplified calculation is not a physical measurement, and buffer settings must follow actual platform accounting.

**Recovery.** Restore the approved active policy, verify both fabrics and correct LUN identity, perform workload I/O, then test supported one-path/fabric loss and return. Record interruption against application timeout. If only one path remains after repair, report degraded service rather than closing the dual-path requirement.

lessons.title: FC zoning, aliases, CFS and active authorization
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Zoning controls which Fibre Channel ports may communicate within a fabric. Use readable device aliases to map operational names to WWPNs, but verify the actual identities behind those aliases. A zone database can contain definitions that are not active. The active zoneset is the policy currently governing the VSAN, so an edit that has not been activated cannot be expected to change access.

Single-initiator zoning narrows the initiator relationships in each zone and simplifies fault containment. It does not replace array masking: zoning authorizes communication with a target port, while the array decides which volumes an initiator may use. Both layers must identify the same intended host. A target can be visible while the correct LUN remains absent.

Cisco Fabric Services distributes supported configuration information and can involve coordinated sessions or locks. A failed or abandoned session can block later changes. Do not clear locks blindly during concurrent work; determine ownership and compare effective state. Fabric-wide changes require a before/after active-policy snapshot and a scoped test because a mistaken alias or zoneset activation can affect many hosts.

### Engineering decisions

**Why does merely defining APP1 not grant access?** APP1 is absent from the active zoneset. Defined configuration and enforced policy are separate states.

**What is wrong with alias db01?** It resolves to the old HBA WWPN. A readable name can conceal an incorrect underlying identity.

**How should the pending CFS session be handled?** Identify and coordinate with its owner before resolving it. Blind clearing can disrupt another administrator's transaction.

**Does zoning replace array LUN masking?** No, they enforce different authorization stages. Target-port communication does not authorize every volume.

**What is a benefit of single-initiator zoning?** Narrower initiator relationships and simpler isolation. It limits unnecessary initiator interactions within a zone.

**Which snapshot is essential before activation?** The current effective zoneset and affected identity mappings. Rollback needs actual enforced state, not just a proposal.

**Why test an unaffected host after the change?** Fabric-wide policy changes can have unintended collateral effects. Acceptance must include scope containment.

**What proves the repair reached the service?** Correct active zoning plus authorized application I/O. Policy activation is necessary but not the final workload outcome.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Continue the shared **MDS SAN construction, identity and active zoning** workbook supplied with this chapter. Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 019. Its file is included among this chapter's starter artifacts.

lessons.title: NPV, NPIV and SAN port roles
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

NPIV allows multiple N-port identities to log in through a single physical fabric port. NPV lets an edge device present attached server identities to an upstream fabric without consuming a full independent fabric-domain role in the same way as a conventional FC switch. The two mechanisms cooperate but are not synonyms: the upstream fabric must support and enable the needed NPIV behaviour.

Port roles express topology. An F-port connects a fabric switch to an N-port device; an E-port forms a switch-to-switch link; NPV uplinks use the appropriate NP role toward upstream F-ports. Trunking can carry multiple VSANs on a supported link, and port channels can aggregate compatible links. A port's physical signal can be healthy while its negotiated role, VSAN or trunk state is wrong.

Design server-to-fabric mapping deliberately. A large NPV edge can concentrate many initiators onto a few uplinks; failure and redistribution may create oversubscription. Separate A/B fabrics should remain independent, including management and maintenance procedures where practical. Do not join the fabrics casually to fix a path-count discrepancy; that can destroy the intended fault boundary.

### Engineering decisions

**Why does only the first server log in?** Upstream NPIV is disabled for the intended multi-identity attachment. The physical link works but additional virtual N-port logins are not supported.

**How do NPV and NPIV differ?** NPV is an edge forwarding architecture; NPIV permits multiple N-port identities. They cooperate but describe different functions.

**What does an E-port normally connect?** FC switches through an interswitch relationship. Its role differs from an end-device fabric attachment.

**Why reject casual A/B fabric merging?** It can remove intended fault-domain independence. Path count is not equivalent to independent fabrics.

**What must an NPV failover test measure?** Surviving login paths and workload capacity after uplink loss. Repinning can preserve connectivity while overloading the remaining uplink.

**Why inspect operational port role?** Carrier-up does not prove the intended FC relationship. Mode mismatch can prevent correct login or fabric adjacency.

**What can a supported FC port channel provide?** Aggregated compatible interswitch bandwidth and member resilience. It still has hashing, compatibility and failure-domain constraints.

**Which design calculation matters for forty concentrated initiators?** Aggregate and failure-state uplink demand. Concentration can create oversubscription despite successful logins.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Continue the shared **MDS SAN construction, identity and active zoning** workbook supplied with this chapter. Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 019. Its file is included among this chapter's starter artifacts.

lessons.title: FC credits, congestion, ISLs and storage maintenance
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Fibre Channel buffer-to-buffer credits limit how many frames a transmitter can send before the receiver returns buffer availability. Credits prevent overrunning the next receiver's buffers; they are not an end-to-end promise that the storage application will be fast. A long link consumes credits while frames and acknowledgments are in flight, so insufficient credits can limit throughput even when the physical line rate is high.

Congestion can propagate from a slow receiver into upstream queues. A zero-credit counter must be interpreted with time, utilization and affected flows: occasional exhaustion under load differs from persistent starvation. CRC or optical errors suggest a different mechanism from a healthy link stalled by unavailable credits. Collect per-port evidence and identify the direction of pressure before replacing hardware.

ISL capacity planning includes normal demand and one-member or one-link failure. FC port channels and traffic engineering can spread exchanges, but not necessarily every single I/O over all members. Storage upgrades require host and array path readiness, compatible firmware and a one-fabric-at-a-time plan where supported. A nondisruptive label does not waive application timeout or path-failover acceptance.

### Engineering decisions

**What does sustained zero transmit credit indicate?** The sender lacks permission to send more frames to that receiver. It suggests buffer pressure but requires contextual diagnosis.

**Can 32 Gb/s surviving capacity carry 50 Gb/s sustained demand without congestion?** No. A live path does not satisfy a demand greater than its capacity.

**Why compare CRC trends with credit counters?** They distinguish corruption evidence from flow-control pressure. Different mechanisms call for different corrective actions.

**Why can long-distance FC need more credits?** More frames remain in flight across the propagation delay. The bandwidth-delay product affects needed buffering.

**What is slow-drain propagation?** A slow receiver causes upstream buffering and pressure. The effect can extend beyond the original endpoint.

**Why check the 30-second application timeout?** Failover must meet the actual service interruption tolerance. Recovered paths may arrive too late for the application.

**What is a sound maintenance sequence for independent fabrics?** Verify the alternate path, change one fabric, validate, then proceed. It preserves a tested service path where the platform supports it.

**Why not increase buffers as the first universal fix?** The cause may be sustained overload or a slow receiver. More buffering can mask or worsen latency without resolving demand.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 019. Its file is included among this chapter's starter artifacts.

Synthetic teaching exhibit. NX-OS examples assume a supported Nexus 9000 10.x lab; APIC examples assume a supported 6.x lab; UCS and MDS exact compatibility must be checked for the chosen release.

Synthetic: a 32-Gb/s ISL is physically clean, with no CRC increase, but transmit credits remain zero for sustained intervals and one target is slow. After losing half of a 64-Gb/s aggregate, offered traffic remains 50 Gb/s. Hosts have a 30-second application timeout.
worked_examples.solution: The clean physical counters make pure optical corruption less likely than congestion/credit pressure, although further evidence is needed. The failure-state capacity is 32 Gb/s, below 50 Gb/s demand; redundancy preserves a path but not the required service. Maintenance must either reduce demand, add capacity or accept a documented degraded service, and path recovery must complete within the application tolerance.

lessons.title: iSCSI, NFS and end-to-end storage path design
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

iSCSI carries SCSI commands over TCP/IP, so storage correctness depends on both the block-storage authorization model and the IP network. Initiator identity, target discovery, authentication where configured, LUN mapping and multipath configuration all matter. A successful TCP connection to a target port is not proof that the intended volume is exposed. NFS supplies file operations and has export, identity, permission and version-specific session semantics rather than the same block-target model.

Place storage paths in explicitly designed subnets and failure domains. Two IP addresses on one adapter and one switch may provide logical alternatives without physical independence. Jumbo frames are optional design choices, not a prerequisite for every storage deployment; inconsistent MTU is worse than a consistent supported smaller MTU. Congestion, retransmission and queueing can dominate I/O latency long before a link fails.

Security must match the protocol and platform. CHAP authenticates an iSCSI relationship but does not by itself encrypt all data. Network isolation, appropriate transport protection, privileged management and storage authorization remain separate controls. Validate failure using real reads and writes on disposable test data, measure recovery time and confirm data identity and integrity after the path returns.

### Engineering decisions

**Why is a reachable TCP/3260 port insufficient?** The target may not map a LUN to the initiator. Transport success precedes storage authorization.

**Are the two sessions physically independent?** No, they share a NIC and switch. Different IP addresses do not remove common hardware dependencies.

**What does CHAP alone provide?** Authentication, not general payload encryption. Confidentiality requires an appropriate separate mechanism.

**Why can MTU inconsistency produce intermittent-looking I/O stalls?** Larger packets may fail on one path while small probes pass. Path and packet-size selection affect symptoms.

**What distinguishes an NFS export check from an iSCSI LUN check?** NFS uses file-service export and permission semantics. Block and file services expose different authorization models.

**What should storage failure testing use?** Disposable representative reads and writes with integrity checks. A ping cannot establish block or file service continuity.

**Why investigate retransmissions during latency spikes?** Loss and congestion can amplify storage response times. A link can remain up while TCP recovery delays I/O.

**What is the safest MTU principle?** Use a consistent supported end-to-end size and verify it. Jumbo size is beneficial only when the whole path supports the design.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Continue the shared **MDS SAN construction, identity and active zoning** workbook supplied with this chapter. Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 019. Its file is included among this chapter's starter artifacts.

lessons.title: AAA, RBAC and management trust across Nexus, UCS and MDS
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Authentication establishes an asserted identity; authorization determines permitted actions; accounting records what occurred. A successful login does not prove that the user receives the intended role. External AAA can return attributes that map to local platform roles, and a mismatch can grant excessive privilege or deny a necessary operation. Nexus, UCS, MDS and APIC have related ideas but different role models and configuration details.

Design administrative access as a service with failure modes. Central AAA improves control and attribution but depends on routing, DNS where used, time, shared secrets or certificates and server availability. A tested local emergency account can support recovery, but it needs restricted access, protected credentials, monitored use and a clear rotation process. Do not weaken normal authorization to make an outage drill easier.

Separate read-only automation from configuration authority. Bind credentials to owners and tasks; avoid shared administrator accounts that erase attribution. Preserve external accounting and platform audit logs with synchronized time. Before a role change, test representative allowed and forbidden commands in a lab or bounded account. A role named operator is not evidence that its effective privileges are limited.

### Engineering decisions

**Why investigate role mapping after successful authentication?** Identity success does not establish correct authorization. Returned attributes may map to an excessive local role.

**What role should the counter-only job receive?** A read scope limited to the required observations. Configuration authority is unnecessary for the task.

**Why specify the management VRF for AAA?** The AAA server is reachable in that routing context. A default-VRF attempt may fail despite physical connectivity.

**What is missing from the emergency-account design?** A controlled test of effective recovery access. An untested account may fail when needed.

**Which test demonstrates least privilege better than login alone?** An allowed action succeeds and an unauthorized change is denied. Positive and negative tests establish the intended boundary.

**Why avoid shared administrator identities?** They weaken attribution and credential lifecycle control. Named owners support investigation and revocation.

**What should accounting evidence contain?** Attributable actions with trustworthy timestamps and outcomes. Useful investigation requires who, what, when and result.

**What must follow emergency credential use?** Review, restore normal control and rotate as required. Recovery access should not become an unmanaged permanent bypass.

Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: First-hop security, routing authentication and MACsec
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

First-hop controls protect assumptions at the host-facing boundary. DHCP snooping distinguishes trusted server-facing paths from untrusted client ports and can build bindings used by other controls. Dynamic ARP Inspection checks ARP claims against trusted binding information or configured exceptions. IP Source Guard applies source restrictions using supported binding mechanisms. A static-addressed host may require deliberate exceptions or bindings; enabling a control without its data dependencies can block legitimate OT or infrastructure endpoints.

Routing-protocol authentication protects adjacency messages against unauthorized participation or alteration within its supported model. A keychain's active lifetime, algorithm and peer agreement matter, as does clock accuracy when time-bound keys rotate. Authentication does not prove the peer's route policy is correct; an authenticated peer can still advertise a harmful route.

MACsec protects Ethernet links between supported peers using cryptographic associations and keys. It is a link-layer protection, not automatically end-to-end encryption across every routed hop. Key agreement, cipher compatibility, replay protection and platform support must align. A link physically up with failed secure association may not carry the intended protected data. Plan key rotation and recovery without silently falling back to unprotected service unless explicitly approved.

### Engineering decisions

**Why can legitimate DHCP fail in the exhibit?** The authorized server-facing path is untrusted. Snooping policy may reject server messages on that boundary.

**Why is the static EPMS host's ARP rejected?** Its legitimate mapping is absent from the trusted validation model. Static addressing needs a supported binding or exception approach.

**What can break time-bound routing-key rotation?** Clock skew and nonoverlapping accepted key lifetimes. Peers can select different valid keys at the same real time.

**Does routing authentication prove route correctness?** No, an authenticated peer can advertise incorrect or harmful routes. Identity/integrity and routing policy are distinct controls.

**What does MACsec primarily protect?** A supported Ethernet link between participating peers. It does not imply encryption across every subsequent hop.

**Why is carrier-up insufficient for MACsec acceptance?** The secure association may be unavailable. Physical and cryptographic operational state are separate.

**What should be tested before broad DAI enforcement?** Legitimate DHCP/static hosts and deliberate spoof rejection. Both availability and the intended security boundary matter.

**When is unprotected fallback acceptable?** Only if explicitly authorized by the requirement and risk decision. A silent downgrade violates the intended confidentiality boundary.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Storage security, fabric binding and management-plane containment
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Storage security has several identity layers. Fabric port security can constrain which devices attach to particular ports; fabric binding can constrain which switches join an authorized fabric; zoning governs port communication; array masking governs volume access. Administrative AAA controls who changes those protections. No single layer substitutes for all the others.

A switch with an unexpected identity joining a SAN can alter the fabric's trust and failure domain even if current host zoning looks correct. Conversely, a legitimate replacement switch or HBA can be blocked by stale binding or port-security policy. The right response is to validate the replacement's provenance and approved identity, then update the narrow relevant control. Disabling all storage security to restore a missing path removes unrelated protections.

Key management also belongs to compute and infrastructure operations. Track purpose, owner, storage, rotation, revocation and recovery for API keys, controller certificates and encryption keys. Availability recovery must preserve confidentiality and integrity requirements. A restored management server with old compromised credentials is not a restored trust boundary. Keep administrative interfaces isolated from ordinary tenant traffic and test that emergency procedures do not create persistent bypasses.

### Engineering decisions

**Which policy most directly explains the replacement switch's rejection?** Fabric binding still references the retired switch identity. The control governs authorized fabric membership.

**Why not modify every host zone first?** The failed identity is the switch membership layer. Changing unrelated authorization expands risk without addressing the stated cause.

**What must precede updating the binding?** Validate the replacement's approved identity and provenance. A mismatch can be a legitimate change or an unauthorized device.

**Why is restoring the exposed BMC token unsafe?** It restores potentially compromised authority. Configuration rollback can reintroduce the original trust failure.

**What does array masking control?** Which volumes are exposed to an initiator. It is distinct from fabric switch membership and zoning.

**What is a port-security check in this context?** Whether the attached FC device identity is allowed on the port. It constrains device attachment.

**What closes trusted recovery after credential exposure?** Revocation or rotation plus verified restricted access and audit evidence. Restoring availability alone is insufficient.

**Why retain independent administrative isolation?** A tenant compromise should not automatically control infrastructure management. Management authority has a much larger blast radius.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

For the BMC, configuration rollback alone would reintroduce exposed authority; revoke or rotate the token and verify management access boundaries before declaring trusted recovery.

lessons.title: ACI architecture, APIC clusters and fabric discovery
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

ACI separates policy management from distributed packet forwarding. APIC controllers manage the policy model and fabric lifecycle; leaf and spine switches perform the fabric's forwarding and control functions. A normal endpoint attaches to a leaf, not a spine. The fabric uses its own infrastructure addressing and control protocols; tenant IP addresses are not a substitute for correctly planned infrastructure pools.

Discovery is a controlled onboarding process. The initially connected leaf is discovered through the appropriate infrastructure mechanism, switches are identified by serial number and assigned intended node IDs, and the fabric extends through the approved topology. Physical discovery does not authorize an unknown switch automatically. Duplicate or incorrect node identities, unsupported cabling, missing discovery adjacency or incompatible software can prevent enrollment. An APIC cluster's membership and health are distinct from a leaf's tenant forwarding state.

Virtual APIC changes controller deployment form and infrastructure dependencies, not the need for a supported resilient controller design. Check the specific supported release, hypervisor/platform constraints, controller sizing, placement and recovery procedure. Losing policy-management access does not imply that every already-programmed packet immediately stops, but it limits the ability to make and assure changes. Do not deliberately remove controllers without the documented maintenance procedure.

### Engineering decisions

**What is the immediate registration defect?** Two leaves are assigned the same node ID. Fabric identities must be unique within the intended scope.

**Where should an ordinary endpoint attach?** A supported leaf access interface. Spines provide fabric transit rather than ordinary endpoint access.

**What does continued traffic during one APIC outage demonstrate?** Existing distributed forwarding survived that observed failure. It does not validate arbitrary controller loss or future policy changes.

**What should authorize a discovered switch?** Approved identity and topology validation. Discovery visibility is not permission to join.

**Why plan infrastructure pools separately from tenant addressing?** They support different fabric functions and scopes. Overlaps or exhaustion can affect fabric operation independently of tenants.

**What changes with virtual APIC?** Controller deployment dependencies and support constraints. The policy-management role remains, with a different hosting model.

**Which evidence helps isolate failed discovery?** Physical adjacency, supported image, node identity and discovery faults. These correspond to the enrollment stages.

**Why preserve cluster quorum during maintenance?** Controller consistency and supported management availability depend on cluster health. A running data plane does not waive controller requirements.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Access-policy chain: pools, domains, AEPs and interface profiles
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

ACI access attachment is a dependency chain. A VLAN pool defines available encapsulation identifiers. A physical or virtual domain relates that encapsulation scope to an attachment model. An attachable access entity profile connects eligible domains to interface policy groups. Interface selectors and profiles associate those groups with actual switch ports, while switch profiles identify the participating leaves. The EPG then needs an appropriate domain relationship and path binding or dynamic attachment.

This separation supports reuse but makes partial configurations easy. An EPG static path using VLAN 620 can be syntactically present while the port's domain chain does not permit VLAN 620. A vPC attachment also requires the supported leaf-pair and bundle policy configuration; selecting a vPC-looking path in an EPG does not build the underlying pair.

Work from physical port upward and EPG downward until the relationships meet. Verify operational encapsulation deployment and fault details, not just whether each object exists. Static and dynamic VLAN allocation modes have different use cases; a manually fixed attachment should not rely on assumptions about a dynamic VMM allocation. Record the exact expected encapsulation on the external device.

### Engineering decisions

**Which dependency blocks the stated attachment?** The VLAN pool excludes 620. The path requests an encapsulation outside the domain's available range.

**What is the AEP's role in this chain?** Relate eligible domains to interface policy groups. It connects reusable domain eligibility to attachments.

**Why can a static binding exist without working forwarding?** Its access-policy dependencies may not resolve. Configured intent can fail deployment.

**What additional foundation does a vPC path need?** A supported leaf pair and vPC interface policy configuration. An EPG path reference does not construct the underlying aggregation.

**Which verification follows the policy repair?** Operational encapsulation deployment and endpoint learning. Object presence alone does not establish effective attachment.

**Why distinguish static and dynamic VLAN allocation?** Their allocation and binding behaviour differ. The attachment method must match the domain and external device assumptions.

**What should remain unchanged during the scoped repair?** Unrelated tenant routing and contracts unless evidence implicates them. Fix the demonstrated access eligibility fault without broad changes.

**What external setting must agree with the deployed encap?** The attached device's VLAN/tagging behaviour. Both ends must classify frames consistently.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Tenant, VRF, bridge domain and EPG boundaries
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

An ACI tenant is a policy and administrative container; a VRF supplies a routing context; a bridge domain defines a Layer-2 forwarding domain and related gateway behaviour; an EPG groups endpoints for policy and attachment. An application profile organizes EPGs. These objects need not have a one-to-one relationship. Several EPGs can share a BD while retaining different policy relationships, and several BDs can share one VRF for routed connectivity.

This flexibility makes naming shortcuts dangerous. An EPG is not simply a VLAN, and a tenant is not automatically a complete physical isolation boundary. Encapsulation identifies attachment; EPG membership drives policy classification; the BD/VRF graph determines forwarding context. Predict a flow by identifying source and destination policy groups, their BDs and VRFs, the forwarding path and the applicable contract model.

Place gateway subnets deliberately. The BD's routing settings and subnet scope interact with external advertisement and shared services. Overlapping addresses can coexist in separate routing contexts but require careful handling when services are shared. Start with a dependency table rather than copying a previous tenant whose hidden defaults may differ.

### Engineering decisions

**What does a VRF separate?** Routing tables and associated routing context. It is not merely a display folder.

**Does a shared BD automatically mean unrestricted inter-EPG access?** No, the EPG policy relationship still applies. Forwarding domain and authorization are distinct.

**Why is an EPG not simply a VLAN?** It is a policy grouping with attachment relationships. Different encapsulations can participate in the logical policy model.

**What connects BD-SERVERS and BD-DATABASE for routing?** Their relationship to VRF BLUE and appropriate routing configuration. Sharing a tenant name alone is insufficient.

**What does an application profile primarily organize?** Related EPGs in the tenant policy hierarchy. It is not the host application's executable image.

**Why record both source and destination EPGs?** Policy classification is directional and relationship-dependent. Knowing only destination IP can miss the authorization context.

**What complicates sharing services between overlapping address spaces?** Address disambiguation and controlled routing/policy boundaries. Separate VRFs permit reuse, but shared reachability requires design.

**Which acceptance evidence is appropriate for the three-tier design?** Allowed application flows and explicitly denied cross-tier flows. Both positive function and policy isolation must be shown.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 028. lessons.title: Contracts, filters, scope, vzAny and preferred groups
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

A contract expresses permitted communication through subjects and filters between policy groups acting as consumers and providers. A filter describes protocol and port matching; contract direction and reverse-port behaviour must be understood for the actual deployment. A route can exist while the contract denies a session. Conversely, an overly broad contract can permit traffic that the routing design happens not to deliver today, leaving a latent exposure when routes later change.

Contract scope limits where the relationship can apply. Shared services and cross-tenant designs require explicit supported relationships; a contract name reused elsewhere is not proof of a common policy object. vzAny applies policy relationships across EPGs within a VRF in a broad way and can simplify design, but it expands the importance of reviewing the affected set. Preferred-group membership can allow communication among included groups according to the feature's model, so it must be treated as a deliberate authorization choice.

For each application, record initiator, responder, protocol, destination service, return behaviour and required inspection. Do not replace an uncertain flow matrix with permit-any. Validate with both expected sessions and adjacent forbidden ports. Where stateful inspection is required, a basic contract filter is not a universal substitute for the chosen firewall service.

### Engineering decisions

**Why does the intended application fail?** The contract permits 443 while the service listens on 8443. Reachability does not override the filter's port condition.

**What is the narrowest justified repair?** Align the approved service definition and filter on 8443. The change should match the required application flow.

**Why is the preferred-group proposal risky?** It changes authorization beyond the single missing service. It can permit broader communication among included groups.

**What makes vzAny powerful and potentially broad?** It can apply relationships across EPGs in the VRF. The affected population must be reviewed.

**What should a filter review include besides destination port?** Protocol, direction, return handling and scope. A single port number is not the entire session policy.

**Does a route prove a session is authorized?** No, forwarding reachability and policy permission are distinct. Both must be satisfied.

**Why test an adjacent forbidden port?** It detects an overbroad rule that also permits the desired service. Positive success alone does not show least privilege.

**When is a service firewall still needed?** When requirements demand inspection beyond the contract's supported filtering. Choose controls for the actual application and threat requirements.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Endpoint Security Groups and membership correctness
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Endpoint Security Groups decouple some security grouping from the EPG's attachment and forwarding organization in supported ACI releases. An endpoint can require a security classification based on configured selectors while its network attachment remains in an EPG/BD structure. This can support segmentation that follows workload identity more naturally than a VLAN-only design.

The security result depends on membership correctness. A selector that unintentionally includes a broad subnet can grant access to unrelated workloads; a missing selector can leave the intended endpoint outside the expected policy group. Inspect effective membership and the supported interaction with EPG contracts, VRF policy and other features for the selected release. Do not assume every historical ACI feature combination has identical ESG support.

Migrations need an explicit policy-equivalence test. Record the old permitted/denied flow set, define the new groups and contracts, observe actual endpoint classification, then compare both positive and negative tests. A GUI object named database is not proof that only database servers belong to it. Stale endpoint information and workload moves can affect the effective classification and must be included in operational checks.

### Engineering decisions

**Why did the development host receive access?** The /24 selector included it in the security group. Authorization follows effective membership, not the intended label.

**What should be repaired?** The selector and verified effective membership. The contract can remain appropriate for the intended group.

**What is the purpose of ESG abstraction?** Separate security grouping from some attachment-based grouping constraints. It supports policy organization beyond a simple VLAN/EPG analogy.

**Why check the exact ACI release?** Supported ESG feature interactions can vary. A design must match available behaviour.

**What best validates migration equivalence?** Compare allowed and denied flows before and after with membership evidence. Desired success alone can hide expanded access.

**Why include workload movement in testing?** Classification must remain correct as endpoint state changes. Static initial membership does not prove lifecycle behaviour.

**Which observation is most useful for the unexpected access?** The development endpoint's effective group membership. It directly tests the classification hypothesis.

**What does a group named DB prove?** Only its configured label until membership and policy are inspected. Labels can differ from effective state.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

worked_examples.scenario:
Synthetic independent engineering case; not captured vendor output.

lessons.title: ACI endpoint learning, proxy lookup and BD forwarding choices
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

ACI learns endpoint identity and location so that traffic can reach the appropriate leaf. Local learning, distributed endpoint information and lookup mechanisms cooperate; stale or conflicting endpoint state can produce symptoms different from a missing contract. Track MAC and IP learning separately because a host can have a learned MAC but no valid IP association for a particular feature.

Bridge-domain settings determine how the fabric handles unknown unicast, ARP and routing. Hardware-proxy behaviour uses fabric endpoint knowledge to avoid ordinary flooding in supported cases; flood mode deliberately replicates unknown traffic within the domain. ARP flooding and unicast-routing settings are independent choices with implications for endpoint discovery and gateway service. Select them from the application and migration requirements, not a blanket belief that flooding is always bad or always necessary.

Troubleshooting begins with classification and location. Confirm the source attachment, source/destination endpoint entries, BD/VRF, applicable policy and actual forwarding path. A silent endpoint may not have advertised enough state for a suppression or proxy expectation; a moved endpoint may leave stale location until the supported learning and aging mechanisms converge. Avoid fabric-wide endpoint clears as the first response: they erase evidence and can create broad relearning bursts.

### Engineering decisions

**Why can a learned MAC coexist with a missing IP binding?** MAC and IP learning state are related but distinct. A function requiring the IP association may still lack needed information.

**Which setting conflicts directly with inter-subnet gateway use?** BD unicast routing is disabled. The expected gateway routing function must be enabled in the design.

**What should be compared after host B moves?** Current and stale endpoint locations with timestamps and learning evidence. A location conflict requires examining effective endpoint state.

**What is hardware-proxy unknown-unicast behaviour intended to use?** Fabric endpoint knowledge to resolve forwarding where supported. It differs from indiscriminate flooding.

**Why avoid a fabric-wide endpoint clear first?** It destroys useful state and can trigger broad relearning. A scoped diagnosis has lower operational impact.

**Can ARP flooding repair a denied contract?** No. Discovery behaviour and authorization are separate policy gates.

**What should determine BD flood settings?** Application discovery, migration and forwarding requirements. Choose supported behaviour based on the actual service.

**Which acceptance test covers endpoint mobility?** Move a test endpoint and verify location convergence plus allowed service. The test must observe both control state and workload effect.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

Clearing every endpoint may briefly hide state but cannot resolve two active sources.

lessons.title: Layer-2 external attachment, STP boundaries and MCP
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Layer-2 external connectivity extends a broadcast domain beyond the fabric and therefore imports external topology assumptions. EPG port bindings define attachment and encapsulation, but external switches still require a loop-safe topology. ACI's fabric does not behave as a conventional single spanning-tree switch for all external designs. Understand which BPDUs are transported or handled by the selected attachment and follow the documented boundary model.

Mis-Cabling Protocol detects certain loops or mis-cabling conditions by recognizing its probes in inappropriate places. It is a protection mechanism, not permission to build arbitrary loops or a substitute for correct external STP/vPC design. A loop can amplify broadcast and unknown traffic, consume buffers and disrupt unrelated services sharing the fabric resources.

Before migration, document native/tagged VLAN behaviour, allowed encapsulations, EPG bindings, external root placement and redundant links. A dual attachment is safe only when its aggregation or spanning-tree model is intentional. Test one link at a time, inspect loop-protection events and confirm that a host does not appear to flap continuously between unexpected ports.

### Engineering decisions

**What do MCP events plus endpoint flapping suggest?** A loop or unintended Layer-2 attachment path. The combined evidence points to topology rather than simple missing routing.

**Why not disable MCP as the repair?** It removes protection without correcting the topology. The underlying loop can remain.

**What must be defined before adding a second trunk?** The supported aggregation or spanning-tree boundary model. Redundancy requires loop-safe forwarding decisions.

**Why check native and tagged VLAN behaviour?** Both sides must classify frames into the intended encapsulation. A mismatch can misplace or drop traffic.

**What does an EPG port binding establish?** The logical attachment and encapsulation relationship. It does not automatically validate the entire external loop topology.

**What should recovery verify after correcting the loop?** Stable endpoint learning, normal traffic rates and required link-failure behaviour. A link-up event alone is insufficient.

**Why can a Layer-2 loop affect other services?** It can consume shared forwarding and buffering resources. Blast radius can exceed the originating host.

**Which evidence should be preserved before changes?** Cabling map, protection events and endpoint movement records. These help distinguish the cause and validate the repair.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: L3Out routing, external EPGs and subnet scope
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

An L3Out connects an ACI VRF to an external routed network through logical node and interface profiles, routing configuration and external policy groups. The border leaf must have a valid physical/path attachment and IP adjacency. A routing neighbor can become established while the desired prefixes remain absent because of advertisement policy, BD subnet scope or route-control configuration.

External EPG subnet definitions have policy-classification purposes as well as routing-related options. Do not assume that defining 0.0.0.0/0 as an external classification automatically creates a default route or advertises every internal subnet. The selected flags and policies matter. A BD subnet intended for external advertisement needs the appropriate scope and L3Out association in the supported design. Contracts between internal and external groups still control authorized traffic.

Diagnose in stages: border interface, routing adjacency, received/advertised prefixes, VRF forwarding, external classification and contract enforcement, then return path. Keep transit routing and inter-VRF leaking as separate advanced topics; the DCACI v1.2 listed L3Out objective explicitly excludes them, while the wider programme may study them elsewhere.

### Engineering decisions

**Why does Established BGP not prove external application access?** Prefixes, forwarding and contracts have additional requirements. Session health is only one stage.

**What is the likely export defect in the exhibit?** The BD subnet lacks the intended external scope/association. The neighbor can be healthy without the desired advertisement.

**Does external EPG 0.0.0.0/0 itself create a default route?** No. Policy classification and routing installation are distinct.

**What should be checked on the external router?** The received internal prefix and return forwarding path. A session needs a usable route back to the source.

**Which objects describe border-node and interface attachment?** L3Out logical node and interface profiles. They connect the routed design to participating leaves and paths.

**What distinguishes a contract failure from missing export?** The route may be present while the authorized flow is denied. Inspect both route state and policy evidence.

**Why keep transit routing scope explicit?** The DCACI v1.2 L3Out objective excludes transit and VRF leaking. The wider programme can add them without mislabeling the exam objective.

**What is a meaningful negative test?** Confirm an unauthorized internal prefix is not exported or reachable as specified. It validates containment as well as desired connectivity.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

### Implementation workbook

Continue the shared **ACI tenant construction and access-policy dependency worksheet** workbook supplied with this chapter. Use the chapter's mechanism and case evidence to complete the relevant construction, fault-isolation and recovery tasks. The complete workbook is taught in chapter 028. Its file is included among this chapter's starter artifacts.

lessons.title: VMM integration, DVS/Nutanix and deployment immediacy
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

VMM integration connects ACI policy to a supported virtualization manager. The domain contains controller connection and credential information, VLAN allocation relationships and integration settings; the hypervisor's virtual switching and physical uplinks must still agree with the fabric access-policy chain. Discovering a VM in inventory does not prove that its port group, encapsulation and leaf attachment are deployed correctly.

Resolution immediacy concerns when policy is resolved against eligible attachments; deployment immediacy concerns when policy is programmed into the relevant hardware. The exact supported options and behaviour must be checked for the selected ACI and VMM release. Immediate and demand-driven choices trade earlier resource use against dependency on discovery and active endpoint state. A VM migration can expose a missing domain/AEP path on the destination host even when the source host works.

VMware vCenter DVS and Nutanix VMM integration are distinct supported integration targets with version-specific prerequisites. Do not assume that one platform's object names, port-group workflow or permission set transfers unchanged to the other. Validate controller authentication, inventory synchronization, dynamic VLAN availability, host uplink attachment and actual migrated workload traffic. Keep VMM credentials scoped to the documented required privileges.

### Engineering decisions

**Why can current VMM inventory coexist with failed VM traffic?** Inventory synchronization does not prove access-policy deployment. The destination attachment can still be incomplete.

**What is the strongest stated H2 fault?** Its access-policy chain lacks the VMM domain relationship. That differs from the working source attachment.

**What risk comes from a nearly exhausted dynamic VLAN pool?** New or changed attachments may lack allocatable encapsulations. Capacity of the policy resource matters.

**What does resolution immediacy concern?** When policy is resolved against eligible attachments. It differs from the timing of hardware programming.

**What does deployment immediacy concern?** When resolved policy is programmed into hardware. The choice affects resource use and demand-driven behaviour.

**Why separate VMware and Nutanix checklists?** Their supported versions, workflows and prerequisites differ. One integration's detailed assumptions are not automatically portable.

**What should a migration acceptance test observe?** Policy deployment and application continuity on both host paths. VM inventory movement alone is insufficient.

**Why scope VMM credentials?** The integration has significant administrative reach. Use required privileges without unnecessary authority.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: Service graphs, redirect policy and stateful path symmetry
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

A service graph describes insertion of a supported network service into an application path. Logical service nodes, connectors, interfaces and device or cluster relationships must match the real appliance topology. Policy-based redirect can steer selected traffic toward service nodes, but successful graph deployment does not prove that the appliance forwards, inspects or preserves the session correctly.

Stateful devices often require both directions of a session to reach compatible state. Asymmetric service paths can create a failure where SYN leaves through one firewall and the return packet reaches another independent state table. Health probes and redirect availability influence failover, but a probe that tests only an interface can miss a broken inspection or downstream path. Define whether failure should fail open, fail closed or use an approved alternate service; this is a requirement decision, not a default convenience.

Troubleshoot source classification, contract/graph association, redirect selection, appliance interfaces and routing, return path and actual session state. Account for NAT where used because it changes the identities seen on each side. A service node can have a healthy management page while its data interfaces are down.

### Engineering decisions

**Why does F2 drop the return packet?** It lacks the session state created on F1. Independent stateful devices may reject asymmetric traffic.

**What is wrong with the existing health evidence?** It tests management/interface reachability but not the required service path. A live appliance can still fail inspection or forwarding.

**What must define fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour?** The approved availability and security requirements. Neither choice is universally correct.

**Which dependency precedes service-node forwarding?** Correct source classification and graph/redirect association. Traffic must first be selected into the intended path.

**Why account for NAT in the packet walk?** It changes addresses and possibly policy/session identities along the path. Observations on opposite sides may refer to translated flows.

**What is a stronger service probe?** A bounded check of the actual required data-path function. It tests more than a management endpoint.

**What should be verified after redirect failover?** Complete sessions, policy enforcement and return-path consistency. A new selected node alone does not prove service continuity.

**Why is bypassing the firewall not an automatic repair?** It can violate the required inspection boundary. Restoring connectivity by dropping security requirements is not acceptance.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

Restore the supported symmetric path or state-sharing design, validate redirect health criteria and test complete application sessions through failure and recovery. Do not simply permit all traffic around the firewalls unless the approved failure policy explicitly allows it.

lessons.title: ACI management access, monitoring and role domains
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Out-of-band management uses a distinct management attachment; in-band management uses fabric connectivity and its associated policy/routing dependencies. Choose both deliberately and verify reachability from authorized sources. A management IP existing in configuration does not mean the path, contract, route and external firewall permit access. Recovery access should remain available under the failures it is intended to repair.

APIC authorization combines roles with security-domain scope. A user can authenticate successfully yet be unable to act on a tenant outside the assigned domain, or can receive broader authority than intended if mapping is wrong. Test exact tenant and operation combinations. Do not solve a scope error by granting universal administration unless that is the approved responsibility.

Syslog, SNMP and Nexus Dashboard Insights provide different observations. Configure time, destinations, credentials and source paths, then verify that representative events arrive and remain attributable. AI-assisted summaries should point back to the actual fault, event and audit records. Monitoring access itself should be scoped and protected; a collector with unrestricted write credentials creates avoidable authority.

### Engineering decisions

**Why can alice authenticate but not modify PROD?** Her configuration authority is scoped to DEV. Authentication and tenant-domain authorization are separate.

**What should precede adding PROD to her scope?** Confirmation that her role is authorized to manage PROD. A denied action may be correct enforcement.

**Why is OOB useful in the incident?** It does not depend on the failed in-band path. Recovery access survives the relevant production failure.

**What proves syslog delivery?** A controlled event arrives with correct identity and time. A configured destination alone is intent.

**Why inspect the syslog source routing context?** The selected context must reach the collector. A route in another VRF may be irrelevant.

**How should an AI-assisted fault summary be used?** As an interpretation linked to inspectable source records. Operators must validate causes and proposed actions.

**What privilege does a monitoring collector normally need?** The narrow read/collection scope required for its function. Write authority should be separately justified.

**What is a meaningful management resilience test?** Lose the specified in-band dependency and recover through authorized OOB access. It exercises the intended failure boundary.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

lessons.title: ACI snapshots, import/export and controlled upgrades
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

ACI configuration snapshots and exported policies support different operational recovery tasks. A local snapshot may help reverse a policy change; an external export provides a separately retained configuration artifact. Neither should be assumed to recreate every operational endpoint entry or every external dependency. Protect exported secrets and record release compatibility and restore procedure.

Upgrade planning covers APIC controllers, fabric switches, hardware support, current faults, target release and the approved upgrade path. Download, policy scheduling, execution and observed running version are different states. Maintenance groups and ordering must respect the supported release procedure and the site's redundancy requirements. Do not infer that all nodes can be upgraded simultaneously because the fabric has multiple spines.

Before the window, resolve material health faults, verify independent backups and OOB recovery, define service probes and abort conditions, and record the pre-change effective state. During execution, follow per-node progress and compare workload behaviour. Afterward, verify running versions, cluster/fabric health, endpoint learning, external routes, policy enforcement and application transactions. Downgrade or rollback support may be constrained; a known-good configuration does not make every software downgrade safe.

### Engineering decisions

**Why is the local snapshot alone insufficient recovery assurance?** It shares controller failure dependencies and may not cover all recovery needs. A separately retained export and tested procedure are required for the intended failure cases.

**What blocks the two leaf models from upgrade approval?** Target-release support has not been established. Unsupported hardware can make the planned transition infeasible.

**Why question simultaneous vPC-pair upgrades?** It can remove both workload attachment paths together. Redundant topology requires compatible maintenance sequencing.

**What should be done with the existing endpoint fault?** Resolve it or explicitly assess its effect before the change. A clean or understood baseline is needed to attribute new failures.

**What does a downloaded target image prove?** The image is staged, subject to integrity verification. It does not prove execution, support or running version.

**Why verify negative policy tests after upgrade?** Security enforcement must survive the software transition. Positive reachability alone can miss an unintended permit.

**Why check fallback support before the window?** Downgrades and configuration compatibility can be constrained. A rollback plan must be executable on the actual versions.

**Which evidence closes the upgrade?** Observed versions, healthy dependencies and validated application/policy behaviour. It connects platform transition to intended service.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.

An image download is not an upgrade readiness gate.

lessons.title: Multi-Pod, Multi-Site and Remote Leaf deployment choices
lessons.body:
### Mechanism and implementation

Multi-Pod, Multi-Site and Remote Leaf address different distribution requirements. Multi-Pod extends one ACI fabric across pods with a supported inter-pod network and a shared administrative fabric model. Multi-Site connects separately controlled fabrics with an orchestration and inter-site design, preserving different control-plane and failure boundaries. Remote Leaf extends supported leaf attachment over an appropriate routed transport while retaining its relationship to the parent fabric. They are not interchangeable labels for any two data centers.

Choose based on latency, scale, failure containment, administrative independence, application mobility and operational recovery. The transport network must satisfy the specific design's routing, MTU, multicast or unicast, bandwidth and support requirements; do not transfer requirements from one mode to another by analogy. Shared policy can simplify operations while also propagating mistakes broadly.

A site-survival claim requires more than fabric reachability. Storage consistency, application dependencies, external routing, DNS, identity services and operator access must also survive. Test partition behaviour: what remains locally functional, what management operations are possible and what happens when connectivity returns? Avoid designing unrestricted Layer-2 extension merely because it is technically possible; bound the need and the fault domain.

### Engineering decisions

**Which requirement most strongly challenges a shared-fabric assumption?** Independent maintenance and local operation during inter-site loss. Control and failure boundaries must match the requirement.

**How does Multi-Site differ conceptually from Multi-Pod?** It connects separately controlled fabrics rather than simply pods of one fabric. The control and failure boundaries differ.

**What does Remote Leaf primarily extend?** Supported leaf attachment relative to a parent fabric. It is not automatically an independent full fabric.

**Why is the 1500-byte interconnect not automatically acceptable?** The selected design's encapsulation and transport requirements must be verified. Ordinary IP reachability does not establish overlay suitability.

**Why does single-site storage limit the resilience claim?** The application still depends on a failed-site resource. Network survival is not whole-service survival.

**What must a partition test examine?** Local service, control operations and reconvergence after reconnection. A brief ping test misses split-state and recovery behaviour.

**Why bound Layer-2 extension?** It extends broadcast and failure domains as well as mobility options. Technical possibility is not sufficient design justification.

**What risk accompanies centralized shared policy?** A mistaken change can propagate across a broad scope. Operational convenience and blast radius must both be assessed.

### Evidence discipline

Predict control-plane state and data-plane behaviour separately. Record the selected hardware, software release, feature support and initial state. Read the supplied exhibit before proposing a change. Compare expected and observed state, use the smallest observation that separates competing hypotheses, and define a recovery trigger before making changes. A successful configuration transaction is not proof of forwarding, workload continuity or restored trust.
